results.title: Cohesion and Coupling in Software with Examples
results.content: Coupling is about connections *across the boundaries* of different modules, while cohesion is about the connections between the *elements inside the boundary* of a module. For a specific functionality to work, it’s difficult to create module which are 100% cohesive, because they might need some parts from other modules. Changing modules with coincidental cohesion is difficult: their elements are independent of each other, so there are big chances they’re used (and therefore coupled) from other modules. Yet, if you consider the two functions as different modules because it’s the good level of abstraction you want to look at, each of these modules is functionally cohesive. * The coupling strength of these connections depends on the number and complexity of the modules’ interfaces, the quantity and nature of the data passed, and if the parts belonging to the different modules often change together. * Creating cohesive modules is the best way to avoid strong coupling. Said differently: loosely coupled modules are often quite cohesive.

Title: Back to Basics: Cohesion and Coupling Part 2 - Simple Programmer
# Back to Basics: Cohesion and Coupling Part 2. Now I want to take a look at the actual application of cohesion and decoupling on software systems. ## Granularity affects cohesion and coupling. **Cohesion and decoupling are completely relative to the granularity of what is a module.**. From here on out, I won’t say class or software or system, I am going to say module when referring to cohesion and coupling. See, the problem is that we need to be able to define what a module is in order to determine if something is loosely coupled or highly cohesive. If we consider a module to be a class, it is not very cohesive at all, since the responsibilities of what should be in a single method or two are spread out across 16. If we consider a module to be an assembly, it still isn’t very cohesive. We have to zoom all the way out to the module is a program level before this software becomes cohesive, but at that level it is very coupled to all the the various other frameworks that it depends on. 1. How we define a module when looking at software affects cohesion and coupling. 2. The granularity we use to build the software affects cohesion and coupling. With that background, we can finally answer the question of whether or not it is possible to achieve high cohesion and loose coupling. There is a point where we have achieved the maximum qualities of loose coupling and high cohesion, and we can try to push decoupling at the cost of cohesion. It is very important that we consider cohesion when we seek to increase decoupling. We have to be conscious of what we are losing in cohesion and understandability when we consider using any kind of framework or pattern to decouple our software. Messaging systems can decouple the different applications that need to communicate with each other making them highly cohesive and very loosely coupled. Figuring out how to appropriately decouple your application while maintaining cohesion is all about figuring out what the ideal size of a module is.

results.content: ## **The Good: Loose Coupling and High Cohesion**. In software design, good coupling translates to loose coupling, where modules. Tight coupling, the antithesis of loose coupling, occurs when modules are. By adhering to principles of loose coupling and high cohesion, developers can. When we hide a module’s “secret” behind a stable interface, we are actively breaking the dependencies that lead to tight coupling. Loose coupling promotes code reusability, as modules can be easily integrated. This promotes loose coupling and makes modules more adaptable. Tight coupling can hinder code reusability, as modules become entangled and. * **Directly accessing internal data of another module:** This creates a tight dependency, making it difficult to modify one module without affecting the other. * **Passing large data structures between modules:** This increases coupling, as changes in the data structure can necessitate modifications in multiple modules. * **Using global variables:** Global variables introduce tight coupling, as any module can access and modify them, making it challenging to track dependencies and changes. If loose coupling is about the relationship *between* modules, high cohesion is about the character *of* a single module. The true power of high cohesion is that it gives a module a **single reason to change**. * **Create modules with a single purpose:** Each module should focus on a specific task or responsibility, promoting cohesion and reducing scattering of functionalities. * **Group related functions together:** Functions that perform related tasks should be grouped within the same module, enhancing cohesion and making code more organised. Low cohesion arises when modules lack a clear purpose and contain elements. Modules with low cohesion can lead to duplication of code, as the same. * **Mixing unrelated functionalities within a module:** This reduces cohesion and makes the module’s purpose unclear. always some degree of coupling between modules in a system. * **Coupling:** The degree of interdependence *between* modules. * **The Goal:** A module should have a single, well-defined reason to change (High Cohesion) and should depend on as few other modules as possible (Loose Coupling). Striving for high cohesion and loose coupling isn’t just a technical exercise; it’s how we validate our design decisions and ensure the module boundaries we create are sound.

results.title: High Cohesion, Low Coupling and Strong Encapsulation · Ben's Blog
results.content: # High Cohesion, Low Coupling and Strong Encapsulation. As a rule of thumb, ensuring software has **high cohesion**, **low Coupling** and **strong Encapsulation** will lead to better quality Object Oriented design. Coupling is essentially how tied a class is to another. The more dependent a class, the higher the coupling. If a class is highly coupled, then a change to one class will cause a number of changes to another, which makes maintenance extremely difficult. Coupling can be reduced by providing a set of interfaces that a client can use to interact with that class. In order to plug the toaster in to the wall socket, the wall socket requires something that has implemented the IPlug interface. It can be an abstract class, an interface or a class’ property. Without abstraction, two parts of the system like our Toaster and wall socket must know about each other directly. The wall socket is tightly coupled to the toaster, therefore we lose out on our coffee or anything else that might require power. Now imagine you are working in a tightly coupled system, and you want to reuse (one of the circles) class. Now imagine you are working in a loosely coupled system, and you want to reuse a class. Cohesion like described above can apply at a class level or it can apply at component / module level. Breaking classes down into smaller, more cohesive units will ensure that their intention is clear, providing a much more cohesive, unified system. This is how we know our class is cohesive. A class square that also has triangles, pentagons etc is not cohesive. Back to software, strong encapsulation would mean interacting with a class by only its public interface. Encapsulation generally will reduce duplication of data and processes in a system as it forces multiple clients to interact via the same interface. The interface could be a data access point or making an Http request but regardless, there should be one and only one implementation for the action in question.

results.title: Modularity in Software Architecture: Cohesion and Coupling Trade-offs
results.content: # How do you evaluate the trade-offs between cohesion and coupling in software modules? Software modules are the building blocks of any program, but how do you design them to achieve optimal performance, maintainability, and reusability? In this article, we will explore the concept of modularity in software architecture and the trade-offs between cohesion and coupling in software modules. Cohesion and coupling are two measures of how well a software module is designed. Cohesion refers to how closely related the elements within a module are, while coupling refers to how much a module depends on or interacts with other modules. Ideally, a software module should have high cohesion and low coupling, meaning that it performs a single and well-defined function and has minimal dependencies and interactions with other modules. There are different ways to evaluate the cohesion and coupling of software modules, depending on the level of abstraction and the criteria of interest. For example, at the code level, one can use metrics such as lines of code, cyclomatic complexity, or fan-in and fan-out to quantify the cohesion and coupling of a module. At the design level, one can use principles such as the single responsibility principle, the open-closed principle, or the interface segregation principle to guide the cohesion and coupling of a module. At the architectural level, one can use patterns such as the layered architecture, the microservices architecture, or the hexagonal architecture to structure the cohesion and coupling of a module. There is no definitive answer to how to balance cohesion and coupling in software modules, as different situations may require different trade-offs. Sometimes, a software module may have low cohesion and high coupling, which can lead to issues such as poor quality, low reusability, and high maintenance costs. In such cases, refactoring the module can be beneficial to improve its cohesion and coupling. Testing is an essential part of software development, as it helps to ensure the correctness, quality, and reliability of a software module. It can also evaluate the cohesion and coupling of a module, as well as identify and fix any issues or defects.
